newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan caretakers tackle tough challenges.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan caretakers tackle tough challenges.

text.p: Pakistan's new caretaker government, backed by military chiefs and the president, sits down on Wednesday to tackle daunting problems after the sudden sacking of prime minister Benazir Bhutto.
Interim Prime Minister Meraj Khalid and his nine ministers were set to hold their first cabinet meeting following Bhutto's abrupt dismissal on Tuesday.

President Farooq Leghari, seeking to reassure foreign investors, said the new government would have to honour a recent accord with the International Monetary Fund for the revival of a much-needed $600 million loan.
The loan aims to plug a financing gap and put Pakistan's wobbly economy back on course.

A visiting IMF team said it would carry on with talks to clinch the loan despite Bhutto's dismissal but cautioned that the deal could be delayed by the change in government or any sign of failure to meet stringent economic targets.
The military, which has ruled the Islamic nation for 24 of the nearly 50 years of independence since 1947, kept a low profile during the transfer of power on Tuesday.

But political observers said Leghari could not have acted without securing approval and cooperation of the generals. Military commanders bedecked with medals attended Khalid's swearing-in ceremony in the presidential palace.
While peaceful, the transfer of power was tinged with apprehension and reflected bitter political divisions.
Bhutto remained a virtual prisoner in her home after Leghari issued a scathing proclamation accusing her government of nepotism, corruption and misrule.

Lawyers for her ex-defence minister filed a court petition claiming that she had been illegally detained, court sources said. Aides to Bhutto said she was in high spirits and ready to fight her dismissal.
Soldiers in the Punjab provincial capital of Lahore detained Bhutto's husband, Asif Ali Zardari, who has been at the centre of corruption allegations.

Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) called the sacking unconstitutional and said party leaders would meet on Wednesday to discuss what it called "the unconstitutional dismissal of the elected government in the darkness of night".
The caretaker government is to supervise early elections President Leghari called for February 3, 1997.
In a televised address late on Tuesday, Leghari said the people were fed up with the inability of successive governments to address their pressing problems.
"There is a national consensus to deal urgently with the declining economy, intolerable law and order situation, pervasive corruption and poor governance," he said.
Addressing critics who said the sacking subverted Pakistan's fledgling democracy, Leghari said he dissolved the lower house of parliament "to save democracy from subversion from within".
Jubilant Pakistanis fired guns in the air to celebrate Bhutto's dismissal.
"This day today is a day of deliverance for the people of Pakistan," opposition leader Nawaz Sharif said.
"I feel that the decision to dismiss the government by the president was absolutely correct because the government had failed completely," cricketeer-turned-politician Imran Khan said.
Other nations took a wait-and-see attitude, saying the transfer of power was Pakistan's internal matter.
Brokers braced for a surge in share prices on the Karachi bourse when trade resumes on Wednesday after a one-day holiday.
"The investors had a perception about Benazir that she was anti-business," Kalim Aziz, research head at Baring Securities, said. "True or not, they will initially react positively."
